transcription.text: So, first of all, thank you so much for coming out to join us at the club. I think, for me,
I was very much motivated as a youngster for some of the things you did, and that led me
to end up with these crazy people in the 19th century. So, everyone's got their own story,
and a big thanks to Lionel. I said I'd buy him dinner if you came along tonight, so I owe him the meal.
Well, I haven't prepared much of a talk other than to talk about amateur radio and adventure,
really, because it's interesting. I've done five flights around the world and a couple
of balloon flights, and amateur radio has had a tremendous effect on the early flights.
These days, of course, with GPS and an Iridium telephone, everything's changed.
And I'm so glad that I did my first two flights around the world before GPS.
The last two flights I've done have been with GPS and Iridium, and it really takes the excitement
out of it, because you know exactly where you are, and you know exactly how much fuel range you've got.
But let me tell you a bit about my first flight around the world.
First of all, a little bit about my background. Many of you would know it.
I was hopeless at school, went to Rosie Public School.
I was in East Roseville rowing a crew and used to come up here walking on my first-class
walks around Terry Hills and out to Roche Creek and places like that.
I was good at two things. One was I loved the outdoors, the Scouts, and the other one,
I loved radio, which we called it in those days.
I used to go into Price's Radio and Angel Place and buy components, and I built a crystal set when I was eight.
I was never any good theoretically, so I suppose people would say I was dyslectic.
I had a speech defect until I was eight years of age, so I used to say my name was Dick Mipf.
Would everyone laugh like you do? Well, to all those people who laughed,
my nice citation aircraft, which I was flying up to Hamilton Island on Friday,
its call sign is Mike India Foxtrot Mipf.
Anyway, I left school and went and worked for Weston Electronics.
My first job was winding coils for the LM18HF transceiver.
Westons were in Sydenham and they made two-way radios, VHF, AM valve radios,
and also HF radios for the Royal Flying Doctor Service and bushfire use.
In those days, I was trying to do the electronics communications certificate course.
Anyone did that? Come on. Oh, good idea. You're geniuses.
I'd asked them a few lectures and realised I wasn't going to be able to get through that,
which I would have loved to. I have no qualifications.
My only qualification is my amateur radio licence, and I'll tell you soon how I got that.
Not that I'd love to have a qualification, but I just didn't have the abilities to be able to do that.
I always worked really hard at understanding things.
Except when I was at school, when I was 14, I built a Noughts and Crosses computer.
I'd been to the powerhouse museum and seen a Noughts and Crosses computer
that was made with valves and inductors and everything.
I built one out of telephone parts, uniselectors and locking relays.
You could play Noughts and Crosses against it and you could never win.
You'd either tie or it would win.
When I worked at Westerns, I used to go out and do installations, and I could do them very quickly.
One day, there was a great kerfuffle at the Western factory.
They said, oh, that radio that's just been brought in, it's made by this terrible bloke called Morrie Finlay.
Anyone ever heard of Morrie Finlay?
And I said, who's Morrie Finlay?
Oh, he was one of the engineers here, but they had to sack him because he stole from us.
I then learned that anyone who left Western Electronics, they always said they sacked them.
And they always said they stole from them.
Of course, Morrie Finlay didn't get sacked and didn't steal.
He opened his own business in Eastern Valley Way, just down there where the old tanneries were,
next to the Gilco building, which is now the Christian Church building.
And I was riding my little motor scooter from where I lived in Coongar Road, Roseville Chase, to Sydney every day.
And I thought, wow, someone making two-way radios just down the road from me, because I lived in Coongar Road.
And so I raced out to the telephone box, no cell phones in those days,
and somehow got through to Finlay Communications and spoke to this Morrie Finlay.
And he said, can you do installations?
And I said, can I ever.
This is, I can give you the exact year, it was 1962, June of 1962.
I did the, I managed to get the living certificate.
And then I left school in 61.
And in 62, started with Westerns in January.
And then in June, I saw the two-way radio, that Morrie Finlay two-way radio.
And so I went to work for Morrie Finlay, and used to do installations, which I was good at,
and just wiring radios and everything.
And I then, through the East Roseville Scouts, I met,
I know it was quite an interesting story here, because he's the clue to starting Dixman Electronics.
When I was working for Morrie Finlay, just to try and get the ham radio licence,
I managed to get my limited call sign, because I had great difficulty learning Morse code,
And Morrie Finlay said to me, oh, one of the investors in this company is a radio ham.
His name is Dr Tony Balthazar.
And so I managed to get his phone number, and I rang him up.
He was a very wealthy bachelor who lived at Point Kuyper.
And I went over and saw him, and at first, he's very strange,
he used to wear a monocle and speak French half the time.
And I became very friendly with him, and I was the first person,
he was an only child, and his parents had just died in that.
Morrie cuddled him the whole life.
He was in the Scouts, but he wasn't allowed to go to Scout camp.
He had some girlfriends, but his mother never approved.
And so finally, he must have been about 45 years of age, and his mum and dad,
his dad was a Belgian consul, his mum was a homemaker, but they were wealthy.
He lived in this beautiful unit at Buckhurst, and he had swan amateur radio gear.
And if you had swan, you were wealthy, you know, wow.
And so I would go around there, and then I talked him into coming to our Scout Hall
at East Roseville, just on Roseville Bridge.
And then 50 years ago, in two weeks' time,
I convinced him to provide the money for us Scouts to sail out to Bowles Pyramid.
And I said, look, it would be great if you provide the money, we can use ham radio.
So we put the swan transceiver on a 50-foot catch,
and we all sailed out to the water.
Hey, you wouldn't be able to do it now.
Attempted to climb Bowles Pyramid, failed, but used ham as a radio.
And when I was out there, Tony Balthazar and I were walking up into Menindee Hill,
and he said, Dick, you've changed my life.
He said, this was in 1964, so I would have been 20 years of age.
And at the time, I was working for Morrie Finlay.
He said, you've changed my life.
I want to pay you to go to university.
And in those days, you had to get a scholarship, or you'd have to pay, sort of thing.
And I said, well, I'd be hopeless at that,
but would you ever loan me the money to start a business?
And he said, well, yes, I would.
Anyway, the next year, he bought me a ticket to go around the world.
And the reason he did that is he wanted to do the Scout climbing course in Candlestick
and wasn't going to do it himself.
And he knew that I would do it with him, so we did that.
Amazingly enough, Morrie Finlay had moved to Gore Hill,
but Western Electronics had moved into the Boots building
next door to Gilko at Eastern Valley Way.
And I always wanted to work close to home.
So I got back from this world trip, and I rang up Westerns,
and I thought, I'll never get anywhere as a technician.
I was a bloody good two-way radio technician.
I can fix radio, so that was one thing I was good at.
I thought I was a complete failure.
All my friends had gone off to university.
I tried to get into DCA when I was 15, and the PMG, all of those things,
and I couldn't get into any of them.
It was amazing, especially when I became chairman of CAA years later.
So here I am, I've come back,
and I thought, I'll never get anywhere as a two-way radio technician
because I don't have any qualifications.
Maybe I could be a salesman.
So I went down to Westerns, and I said,
I'd like to apply for a job as a two-way radio salesman.
And they said, no, no, you know nothing about two-way radio sales,
and we want you as a technician.
And in those days, you were never without a job.
And so I applied for a couple of jobs.
I was thinking of joining the National Parks,
and luckily for me, it was the year that National Parks Rangers
had to have a degree, for some bloody reason.
So I didn't get into that.
And I was just about to ring Westerns and say,
I'll take the job as a technician, fixing two-way radios.
Because they had the contract for manly cabs,
which were AM in those days, old valve equipment.
And Westerns rang me up and said,
oh, we'll give you a go as a salesman.
And for the first... I was called a sales engineer.
Can you imagine? I've still got the card.
I wasn't an engineer, but it sounded good.
And for the first six months, I couldn't sell anything.
But after a while, I started to work out how to be a good salesman.
And in the end, after about 18 months,
I started selling enormous amounts of two-way radios.
because we were selling AM radios, valve equipment,
and SCC had come up with their beautiful 151 series.
And I tried to talk Westerns into making a solid-state unit,
And I remember I was so disillusioned,
I went down to GKN Building and Engineering,
and they were looking at a quote from Western Electronics and from STC.
And the obvious thing for them to buy would be STC equipment.
It was so superior. FM, solid-state, 25 watt.
And I had this crappy little 5 watt Western Electronics LN230,
But I got the sale, and they brought 50 of these radios,
and I was the hero, but I thought,
oh, I don't really like this.
And I remember saying to Alan Walker, who ran Westerns,
and he ended up coming to work for me at Dick Smith's,
I said, look, I don't really like this.
And he said, oh, if you're a good salesman,
you have to be loyal to your company.
we're no longer going to fix the radios for manly cabs.
And I sort of saw my opportunity.
Now, they'd made a terrible mistake.
When I was going around as a salesman,
oh, we want to get you as a salesman.
We've heard you've been selling a lot, and we'll provide a car.
Now, up until then, I'd been 18 months,
I could never save any money, because as you know,
in those days, you'd get 30 quid a week or $30 or something,
$60, and you'd spend it all on your car.
And I had a car on high purchase and all the rest of it.
And so Vinton offered me the job with the car,
so I said to Westerns, I had no intention of taking the job.
I'd been offered a job by Vinton, they're going to give me a car.
And very quickly, Westerns said, we'll give you a car.
So they gave me a car.
It was the greatest mistake they could have ever made,
because for the first time in my life, I saved some money.
And after about four or five months, I had $600.
I always remember this, and my fiancée at the time,
Pippi McManamie, from Bayview Girl Guides or whatever it was,
I always mention this, because we started Dicksmith Electronics
And if ever we get divorced, that's how I've divided up.
Anyway, she puts in her $10, because she's still at school.
And I put in my $600, because Westerns had stupidly given me this car,
And I said to Westerns, I'm going to leave and start a business
fixing the Manly cab two-way radios.
I started the business down, well, initially at the Big Bear
at Neutral Bay, underneath the car park, $15 a week rent,
And I got the agency for SDC 151 two-way radios.
And I sold a lot of two-way radios, because I really believed in them,
and they were the best and state-of-the-art thing.
Sold a lot to ABC cabs, and sold them to business people
Now, where the story gets exciting, I then moved from,
about after seven months at the Big Bear, I moved up to Gore Hill.
And I was servicing two-way radios, selling car radios,
and one day I went into the city to George Brown's.
Anyone remember George Brown? Put up your hand.
Now, George Brown was a typical wholesaler, electronic parts wholesaler.
You'd have up to a dozen people behind the counter.
The service was so bad, you'd have fistfights,
because, you know, who was going to be served next?
And I remember thinking, wow, if these people are so hopeless
and they've got so many customers there, I should get into
And so I rented a little house for about $20 a week
just down from the Wireless Institute of Australia.
And I started Dick Smith Wholesale, selling electronic components.
Stupidly, I put on a manager, and he's off-sided,
who I knew very little about,
and put $15,000 into it, bought all this stock.
And about four months or five months after we started,
we started doing a bit of business.
It was always the conventional way, everything on a counter.
You'd come in, one resistor, eight cents,
You'd calculate and write out this bloody great docket.
I'm leaving, and the off-siders said, I'm resigning too.
And I thought that was ridiculous. And why are you leaving?
And so I had to go down and run the business myself.
And about two weeks later, at about 11 o'clock at night,
I suddenly realised that the manager had stolen 15 grand's worth of stock.
What he had done is he knew that George Brown
and various companies like that would not send the invoices
until the end of the month.
And so he bought all his stock.
and it was only when I'd found an envelope with invoices,
and I thought it had some very expensive silicon control rectifiers,
and I went to the bin, and there weren't any there.
And I started going through all the boxes,
and I realised I'd been conned.
I rang up the police, and the name, Bill Mostyn,
They've never had a conviction against him,
They immediately got a search warrant for his house,
and based on his house, he's got boxes of electronic components.
But he had receipts from the Jeff K Gray auction house
And there was no way of proving where the bombs came from.
Now, that terrible thing was the best thing
that could have ever happened to me,
considering I only put 15 grand in the business,
it was in a terrible state.
It was going to go broke.
And my accountant said, oh, you should liquidate the business.
To this day, I can't read a balance sheet.
But I said, what does liquidate mean?
He says, oh, you just close it down and sell all the stock off.
And I said, well, what's going to happen to the money that's lost?
He said, well, that's bad luck.
The people who gave you credit, they'll lose their money.
And I remember thinking, because of my background in the Scouts,
and I suppose my parents, I said,
well, but how will I live with myself?
You know, Dick Smith, old style, going broke.
And my accountant said, well, that's just life.
You've had the stock stolen, it's well known,
and there's nothing they can do about it.
And then he saw my concern,
and he said, well, one thing you could do
is you could appoint a receiver.
And he said, that's a firm of accountants
who can run the company with you
And I said, well, that's what I'll do.
I reckon I could do it in about two and a half, three years,
and I'll close the money business down.
I said, that was a really sensible lesson.
Don't start up something that you know nothing about.
And I'll stick to the car radios and two-way radios
like the dashboard sticks and radios and everything.
Now, I'm not a religious person,
but there is a God there.
I believe in karma, do the right thing
and the right thing happens to you.
When I'm down there behind the counter,
there was a company called Kitsets that had just started.
And Kitsets were selling electronic components,
They didn't have all this tax crap and all the rest of it.
And they were doing really well by mail order.
And I looked at this crazy load of things
and I thought, gee, if we just pay the tax...
I remember I got in touch with the tax department.
They said, well, to pay the tax on all your goods,
I've virtually never borrowed any money in my life
and I loaned him about three grand
to start the car radio and two-way radio business.
But I borrowed the money from custom credit,
and then started selling, in effect, retail,
which is what every business is now.
And I also bought our little catalogue
called the First Dick Smith Catalogue,
which I had a coupon in Electronics Australia magazine.
I remember I went down to get the catalogue printed.
I took the photos myself with a box-branded camera,
I got it printed very cheaply,
and they cost 12 cents a copy or something.
We were selling them for 50 cents in an ad in EA.
And the bloke who was the printer,
He said, you'll never sell catalogue.
You'll be lucky to give them away.
So I changed the order from 10,000 to 5,000 or 3,000 or something,
To cut a long story short, within about 12 months,
we were making more money out of catalogue
And the business just started to boom.
And down there in that little Atchison Street,
I then realised I'd closed the car radio business.
First of all, we moved Dick Smith Wholesale
up into the flats next door to the car radio business.
And then one day I said to my staff,
I'm going to wind down the shutter.
I'm going to put huger carpet tiles in a lowered ceiling
I took a cheap ticket around the world
and found that there was Lafayette and Radio Shack
and Heathgate and places like that
were selling components a different way.
And so we put it all out in bins
and the type of a J-car now that you look at,
the first year I'm going to turn a million dollars over
because I'd come in on a Sunday morning.
There would be 50 people lined up
And then the most fortuitous thing happened.
and most of what we sold was locally made,
I made selected cooling equipment and power supplies.
Gough Whitlam's taken all the duty off everything.
how can you be helping Australian farmers?
You wrecked the Australian electronics industry.
I was part of the Aussie electronics industry
when Whitlam took the duty off
and very quickly all of these companies closed.
AWA, Ducombe, Plessy, all the manufacturers closed.
And so I started buying from importers,
but very quickly I couldn't get enough stock.
So I went overseas to Japan
and it just opened up my eyes.
Then I think the yen to the dollar now
is about 75 yen to an Aussie dollar.
Then it was 425 yen for the Aussie dollar.
So we could buy stuff in just so cheaply.
Our first container load came in
Dixner Electronics went from a tiny business
But when I got to about 500 staff,
most people think if you're wealthy,
your plan was always to be wealthy.
Well, I never had that plan.
I thought whenever I become wealthy,
I'll share it with all my staff.
The interesting thing was in the early days,
I had all these bonus systems,
but some people are not motivated by bonuses
and when we had a bad month,
And I'd say, why are you resigning?
Oh, I'm not getting my bonus.
well, that's because our turnover's way down.
Oh, well, you can afford to pay it.
And it was, I really learnt
that there are people who are motivated by incentive
and there are people who would like a nice,
steady job with a guaranteed income.
So I learnt lots of those things on the way.
we moved from the Gore Hill,
when I sold it to Woolworths in 1982,
and the net profit was 8 million.
So we were making 25 cents net in the dollar.
Woolworths today make about two and a half cents
But it was because it was completely vertically integrated.
We would buy directly from Japan
and we didn't sell anything you can compare a price with.
We had the Dixon system, 80 computer.
People said, why don't you sell Apple,
and I wanted to run a business that would last,
that I could pay the staff and that could do well.
And when I got to that 50 million turnover,
I said, I'm going to sell out,
and spend more time with my family.
I was treated as an eccentric
because at the time my cat said,
you can become a Rupert Murdoch.
Rupert had just moved to England
and I realised the formula that we had
could be repeated right around the world
with the catalogues and all the rest of it.
But I didn't want to do that.
I sold out to Woolworths for over 20 million dollars
and I was 36 years of age
and I wanted to then do other things
and I went on and flew around the world
and now I have Gixsmith Foods,
which is sort of a charitable thing.
But I want to get onto my venture.
So what I wanted to do was to go venturing
and originally I'd learnt to fly
when I was running Gixsmith Electronics.
it was a nice friendly company.
Everyone's come to your lectures now.
He's looking for some Gixsmith friends.
Is this boring or am I going too far?
and I just started to go venturing.
I'd learnt to fly right at the time,
just after Gixsmith also went into receivership.
I was really worried and I was working seven days a week
but I found out you could go out to Hoxton Airport
and for $22 an hour you could learn to fly.
So I learnt to fly a little Cherokee
you bloody thing, there's always wings.
There were low wing planes I learnt to fly
and so you could never see much anyway.
there was never an instrument nearby,
So I didn't really like it that much.
But I then bought a little twin Comanche plane
and then one day I thought I could never get an instrument rating
because of my dyslexia and difficulty in learning things.
I looked at the study papers for the instrument rating
which are just double Dutch even today
but I do have an instrument rating now, I don't know how I got it.
But I looked at the papers
and I thought I'll never get an instrument rating
so I have to fly visually everywhere.
And one day I was flying back from Tasmania
the kids probably then were six and seven or something
and I got stranded at Narrandera Airport
and I have to ring up Bankstown
to get a pilot to fly a plane up
with another pilot to fly my plane back with my family
because I couldn't fly in the bloody cloud.
I hear thump, thump, thump, thump, thump, thump
and a helicopter comes in on my hands
and it was a chap called Chick Barrett
in the Electricity Commission Jet Ranger.
And I walked over to him and I said
wow, is this an instrument rated helicopter?
He looked at me and said no!
He said with a helicopter you just fly under the cloud
and he said if the cloud gets too low
you land and have a cup of tea with somebody.
If you knew me, that's me, that's my type of flying.
So, finally got flown back the next day to Sydney
and we were running Nick Smith poll
at the head office from Carlisle Street
and I rang up Bell Helicopters
and business was making about a million dollars a year profit
I said I want to buy a helicopter
and then went up with an instructor
and picked it up from the Brisbane Bell place
flew it down to my farm at Ross Glen
and in three weeks learned to fly the damn thing.
I mean a helicopter is the most amazing thing.
It is the ultimate off-road vehicle.
And I always thought because I had fixed-wing aircraft
the tradition was you bought a fixed-wing aircraft in America
and you flew it back across the Pacific Ocean
put in good tanks like King's was good
and that was a dream of mine.
When I got into helicopters that was not possible
but I'd worked out maybe if you put a big tank in it
you could fly it home to Australia via the UK
and then down through Europe to Australia.
if you're going to fly that far why don't you fly around the world?
And I said well you can't fly around the world
because you can't get across the Pacific Ocean.
and in those days it was the time of the Cold War.
All the original solo flights and fixed-wing flights
by Wiley Post around the world had just gone through Russia
and the crossing of the Pacific is 60 miles on the Bering Strait
But then I looked at it and thought
well surely the Russians would give me approval
and so I had this plan and I thought
if I don't get approval from the Russians
I'll try and put some fuel on a ship and land on the ship
but I thought I'll never have to do that
because I'll get approval from the Russians.
Now I realised that for the helicopter flight around the world
but I couldn't do the Morse code
and I tried and tried and tried
and in the end a chap called Bill Storer
French as Forrest. He's still alive today.
Bill, for some reason he felt sorry for me
so he came to my house and he tested my Morse code
because you were supposed to do 13 words a minute or something?
Well I went da da da
and he, not corruptly, realised it was better that I be alive
because you couldn't have an HF radio.
In those days you had to have Morse code.
Now we use Morse code but...
Can you imagine me flying my helicopter?
Da da dee da da da
I don't know how it worked out
but you're supposed to go in to get your Morse code done
and it's getting closer and closer to my departure
I don't have my full call sign
and I really need it to be safe on this trip
and no satellite phones in those days
and he said I'll come around to your house and I'll test you
and I said oh I'm not very good.
Anyway, da da da, and he gave me my licence
about 30 years after that flight around the world
we had a talk in at the Paris Museum
and I was able to thank him for giving me that licence.
And so the trip around the world in the helicopter
and this is getting about what my talk's about
because first of all I was solo and I was very inexperienced
I'd only done 700 hours in a helicopter
and I visualised that I would always fly in good weather
but one of the first mistakes I made was
I said look I've heard Prince Charles' helicopter part
I said if I can get my helicopter to England
I was going to take off from the Bell factory at Fort Worth
it'll be the first solo crossing of the Atlantic
I said the first solo by fixed wing aircraft was Lindbergh
I said this will be the first rotary wing
and it'll be by an Australian
normally the Americans hold just about every absolute record
and so Malcolm Fraser rode off to Prince Charles
and he came back, yeah fantastic
and he said on some holidays in Murramurra Castle
tell Mr Smith to call in
so we worked out this date
the 12th of August or something I'd planned up
now that was an enormous mistake
because I'd planned to fly the Atlantic
in the middle of a high pressure system
I got into a low pressure system
I couldn't believe you could fly in
and imagine if you're with me
the whole back of it is fuel
200 gallons of fuel instead of 90 gallons
I've got a little life raft sitting beside me
a life jacket on, no floats on the helicopter
because if you put floats on you don't get the range
but it is a very reliable engine
and I had a survival suit on
so once you left the continent to fly over the water
you didn't have a clue what ground speed you were doing
and I remember the day I took off from Greenland
and I got into weather so bad
I'm winding in and out through snow storms and snow flurries
down below me is a 50 to 80 knot gale
and it's blowing bits of icebergs off the top of each other
I told everyone, I've found an engine pilot
I just auto-rotate a helicopter glides
and then I'll roll the helicopter and lift and climb out into my life raft
I looked down and I thought
it was freezing, the water was on
I was going to live about one second
and I had a little Super 8 camera to talk to
because ingrained in me from a kid was
you must always have a work ethic
and so even though I could afford to fly around the world
I decided I would make a documentary film
and make the thing a working holiday
which it was in the end
and I pre-sold the films to Channel T in Sydney
and it's interesting, when I played the film back
my editor said, oh it's a problem
when you're about halfway across the Atlantic
there's a fault with the audio
and in fact the audio, there was a tremor in my voice
and I was talking to the camera to try and get some confidence
I thought I'll never get through to Reykjavik in Iceland
the needle, I'm trying to track in on a radio station there
but because there were so much storms around
the needles are wavering like this
so I decided I think I should go back
I was just at my point of no return
I'd better go back to Greenland
so I called up a high-flying airline
now I did have the emitter radio
and from Iceland on I spoke to
the Yazoo agents in Matlock, Lowe's
but for some reason I couldn't get HF contact there
so I didn't have any contact
I went on to the guard frequency
who was obviously way up flying the Atlantic
I'm trying to get into Iceland
but the weather's too bad here
I'm going to go back to Greenland
can you check the weather in Greenland?
and they came back and they said
no no the weather's closed in Greenland
you won't be able to get back there
we recommend you go to Shenwick
and I'm trying to explain to him
and he just doesn't believe me
and they're looking down at this weather
we think if you keep persevering towards Iceland
so I'm whining in and out
and I don't know how much fuel I've got
I think if I get out of this alive
I'll have to come up with some excuse
because I'd had quite a lot of publicity of leaving
and Dick Smith's going to attempt to fly around the world
and so I was thinking of this incredible excuse
and say oh I'm going to ship the helicopter back
and there's a problem mechanically or something
and as I actually got to the airport
there was a ray of sunlight
through an opening in the cloud
so I tracked up and I landed there
and I remember I was just absolutely scared
